question.text: A 55-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-week history of tingling pain in the sole of his right foot when he raises it above chest level during exercises. He reports that he started exercising regularly 2 months ago and that his right calf cramps when he uses the incline feature on the treadmill, forcing him to take frequent breaks. The pain completely disappears after resting for a few minutes. He has an 8-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus. He has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 34 years. His only medication is metformin. His pulse is 82/min, and blood pressure is 170/92 mm Hg. Straight leg raise test elicits pallor and tingling pain in the right foot. There is no pain in the back. His muscle strength is normal. Femoral pulses are palpable; right pedal pulses are absent. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.B: Acute thrombosis of right popliteal vein
options.F: I don't know or cannot answer

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The patient's symptoms of pain in the right foot when raising it above chest level, along with absent right pedal pulses, strongly suggest vascular insufficiency. The history of diabetes and smoking further increases the likelihood of peripheral artery disease (PAD). The calf cramps during exercise are also a classic symptom of claudication, which is caused by insufficient blood flow to the muscles during activity.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: Absent right pedal pulses and claudication symptoms (pain in the foot with exercise relieved by rest) are highly indicative of peripheral artery disease.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: B: Acute thrombosis of right popliteal vein is less likely because the symptoms are chronic (6 weeks) and relieved by rest, not acute. C: Lumbar spinal stenosis can cause leg pain, but the absence of back pain and normal muscle strength make this less likely. D: Aortoiliac artery stenosis is possible, but the symptoms are more localized to the lower leg and foot, making femoropopliteal stenosis a more probable diagnosis. E: None of the above is incorrect because option A is the most likely diagnosis.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The patient's symptoms of intermittent claudication with pain in the foot during exercise, pallor, and absent pedal pulses suggest peripheral arterial disease. The straight leg raise test eliciting pain and pallor further supports arterial insufficiency. The absence of back pain and normal muscle strength reduces the likelihood of spinal stenosis. The patient's history of smoking and diabetes increases the risk of atherosclerosis, making arterial stenosis more likely than venous thrombosis. The femoral pulses are palpable, but the pedal pulses are absent, indicating a lesion below the femoral level. Femoropopliteal artery stenosis fits this pattern.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: Absent pedal pulses with palpable femoral pulses
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: Lumbar spinal stenosis was considered but ruled out due to absence of back pain and normal muscle strength. Acute thrombosis of the popliteal vein was ruled out because the symptoms are more consistent with arterial rather than venous disease. Aortoiliac artery stenosis was less likely due to the location of symptoms in the lower extremity and the absence of pain in the back.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The patient presents with neurogenic claudication-like symptoms — tingling pain in the foot provoked by raising the leg, relieved by rest, and associated with straight leg raise test pallor — which are classic for lumbar spinal stenosis. The absence of back pain and normal muscle strength further support a neurogenic rather than vascular cause. The vascular findings (absent pedal pulses) are secondary to the neurogenic compression and not the primary cause of symptoms.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: Straight leg raise test elicits pallor and tingling pain in the right foot, with no back pain and normal muscle strength — classic for lumbar spinal stenosis.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Vascular causes (A, D) were considered but ruled out by the absence of typical vascular symptoms (e.g., rest pain, ischemic ulcers) and the fact that symptoms are positional and relieved by rest. Acute thrombosis (B) is unlikely given the chronicity and absence of swelling or acute signs. None of the above (E) was considered because the clinical picture strongly supports lumbar spinal stenosis.

olmo3_7b.differential_considered: B (thrombosis) could cause sudden pain and pulse changes, but the chronicity and risk factors (diabetes, smoking) point more to vascular stenosis rather than acute thrombus. C (spinal stenosis) typically causes myelopathy, not foot ischemia. D (aortoiliac stenosis) is less specific for foot symptoms. E is only chosen if no diagnosis fits, but A is the best fit here.
